analysis.one_liner: Bars employers from hiring permanent strikebreakers during the first twelve weeks of an economic strike.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee markup or a House floor vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current labor law, an employer may hire permanent replacement workers during an economic strike, meaning striking workers can lose their jobs simply for striking. This bill would have made that an unfair labor practice for the first twelve weeks of a strike under both the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act, and would have barred employers from giving hiring preferences to strikebreakers over strikers who had unconditionally offered to return to work. It also would have required the National Labor Relations Board to fast-track investigations of such cases so a complaint could issue within the twelve-week window.
analysis.who_benefits: Striking workers and their unions. The bill would have guaranteed strikers a twelve-week window in which their employer could not permanently replace them, and would have required that strikers who offered to return be given hiring priority over strikebreakers. It also would have covered railroad and airline workers under the Railway Labor Act, whose strikes are governed by different rules.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unfair labor practice for an employer to grant permanent replacement status to anyone performing bargaining unit work during an economic strike for a twelve-week period beginning with the first replacement hire [S3].

Bars employers from giving any employment preference to workers who crossed the picket line or offered to work over strikers who exercised protected rights and have unconditionally offered to return to work [S3].
Applies the same restrictions to railroad and airline carriers under the Railway Labor Act, covering workers in industries governed by separate labor law [S3].

Requires the NLRB to give priority to preliminary investigations of unfair labor practice charges filed before a replacement is hired, and to try to issue a complaint before the twelve-week window closes [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially in strike-prone industries, who would lose their most powerful lever against a strike: the threat to permanently replace striking workers. Rail and airline carriers, and employers generally, would have to settle disputes with their existing workforce during the first twelve weeks of a strike rather than hire permanent replacements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers, especially rail and airline carriers

drawbacks.text: The twelve-week limit is temporary: after the window closes, an employer could still permanently replace economic strikers, so the bill caps but does not end the practice [S3].

Employers and business groups argued that restricting the ability to hire replacements reduces employer leverage in negotiations and could make prolonged strikes more likely or more costly to resolve — the standard objection to striker-replacement restrictions (general knowledge about the mechanism of strike leverage; no provided source states the business position).

The expedited NLRB procedure would push the agency to reach judgment on charges within twelve weeks, which critics of fast-track labor cases generally warn can strain the board's capacity (general knowledge about NLRB case processing; no provided source addresses it).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers the bill covers, the benefit is real and concrete: a protected period during which walking a strike line does not mean permanently losing your job. The bill's limits are worth stating plainly — it protects strikers for twelve weeks only, after which permanent replacement remains lawful, and it relies on an already backlogged labor board to move fast enough for that protection to matter in practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to its Labor-Management Relations subcommittee, where it sat with no further action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Ridge introduced the bill on July 16, 1991, joined by three Republican cosponsors [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced [S5].
On August 13, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations — the last action of any kind recorded for the bill [S5].
No committee vote, floor vote, or further action ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers — including rail and airline carriers — are better off, because the existing right to permanently replace economic strikers was left untouched. The workers who might have used this protection never got a vote on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, who kept the replacement-worker tool

for.name: Rep. Tom Ridge
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Collective Bargaining Protection Act of 1991 on July 16, 1991.

for.name: Rep. Amo Houghton, Rep. Olympia Snowe, and Rep. Ralph Regula
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no further recorded action by any of them.

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on July 16, 1991, and referred it to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations on August 13, 1991; never held a markup or reported the bill to the floor.

against.name: Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after August 13, 1991, with no hearings, markup, or vote recorded for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was entirely Republican-sponsored — Rep. Ridge and three Republican cosponsors from Northeastern moderate districts [S4] — and no recorded opposition vote ever occurred because the Democratic-led committee never acted on it [S5].

industries.industry: Employers (generally, including manufacturing and service firms with unionized workforces)
industries.note: Under current law an employer facing an economic strike may hire permanent replacements; the bill would have barred that for twelve weeks and stripped strikebreakers of hiring preferences. This matters to workers because permanent replacement is what turns a strike into a permanent job loss.

industries.industry: Railroads and airlines (carriers under the Railway Labor Act)
industries.note: The bill applied the same twelve-week replacement ban and anti-preference rule to carriers under the Railway Labor Act, whose strikes follow separate procedures.

Unions' core leverage in an economic strike is withdrawing labor; guaranteeing a protected period removes the employer's main counter-threat and strengthens the union's bargaining position on behalf of its members.
